newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German bankers bet on punctual EMU start.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German bankers bet on punctual EMU start.

text.p: Germany's most influential banking federation on Monday brushed aside talk of a possible delay to the start of European monetary union, saying postponement would be disastrous for financial markets and the economy.
"We must do everything to ensure that there is no need for any delay (of EMU)," Karl-Heinz Wessel, president of the BdB banking federation, told a news conference.
"I would be most unhappy with any such development. It would cause significant (market) upheaval and hurt our economic prospects," Wessel said.

Speculation that the launch of Europe's planned common currency may have to be postponed until after the January 1 1999 deadline -- a nightmare scenario for the staunchly pro-euro German banks -- has been growing in recent weeks.
Germany has been regarded as a hardliner on the Maastricht treaty, which specifies a January 1999 start.

But its position was blurred this weekend as Finance Minister Theo Waigel was quoted in the Bild newspaper as saying that fulfilling the Maastricht convergence criteria was more important than the EMU timetable.
The BdB said there was no reason to suspect that Germany would not fulfil the budgetary, inflation and exchange rate criteria set down by Maastricht.

Noting that Waigel and sundry representatives of the powerful Bundesbank believed Germany could hold its budget deficit below three percent of GDP in 1997, as the Maastricht Treaty calls for, Wessel said there were grounds for optimism.
"We have quite a way to go before the final decision is reached on who qualifies for EMU. And the authorities tell us we are on the right track," Wessel said.

Turning to the practical issues surrounding EMU, the BdB reissued a familiar cry from German banks to abolish the non-interest-bearing deposits they must leave with the Bundesbank as security -- the much-hated minimum reserves.
"If minimum reserves apply to the euro-zone, then people are simply going to look for business in other financial centres. This is something we can't afford," said Wessel.

No decision has yet been taken on whether the future European Central Bank will use minimum reserves, but the Bundesbank is urging that it do so, to the chagrin of banks which view them as an unacceptable competitive disadvantage.

Wessel also called on Germany to convert its stock of mark-denominated government debt to euros from January 1 1999, thus keeping up with rival financial centres such as France which have already declared plans to do so.
No firm decision has been taken on this issue in Germany, although one is expected soon. Early conversion is considered crucial to maintain Germany's role as a liquid and attractive financial centre.

On the economy, Wessel said the BdB concurred with the official German forecast for 2.5 percent growth this year, but noted that the country's gross domestic product was not keeping pace with developments in gross national product.

Stronger spending on infrastructure provided a "glimmer of hope", Wessel said, but investments were still weak and a stabilisation on the jobs market -- where unemployment is at a post-war high -- was unlikely until the second half of 1997.

"The jobs market is a source of major concern," Wessel said, but he blamed the record jobless tally of 4.7 million in February largely on structural problems in Germany rather than economic weaknesss.
"As long as Germany retains its top position internationally on wages and supplementary wage costs as well as corporate taxes, nothing much will change," said Wessel.

The BdB represents the interests of all leading German commerciall banks. As of Monday, Commerzbank AG chief executive Martin Kohlhaussen officially succeeds Wessel, a co-owner of private bank Sal. Oppenheim, as its president.
